Hi Alex —

Thanks for the clear questions. Below is a concise mapping and pointers to the artifacts we typically attach to SIG responses. I kept it short so your procurement team can paste into the SIG fields; let me know if you want expanded language.

1) High-level responsibility split (one-paragraph each):
- Hosted (Redwood API): Redwood operates the full control plane and serving runtime. Customer data is encrypted in transit and at rest; customers do not have direct access to host-level keys. We provide per-tenant logical isolation, customer-level access controls, and token/role-based admin controls. Evidence: redwood-soc2-report-2026.pdf (SOC 2 scope and auditor statement), hosted-dedicated-private-matrix.pdf (row for Hosted), and the network diagram.

- Dedicated (Reserved Capacity): Customer has a dedicated GPU pool and logical isolation at the compute layer; Redwood continues to operate the control plane unless the customer elects a Private control plane. Data plane separation: model inference happens on tenant-dedicated hosts; telemetry and management signals are forwarded to Redwood-managed control plane. For customers requiring stronger separation, we support an option to restrict telemetry forwarding (contracted). Evidence: hosted-dedicated-private-matrix.pdf, audit log sampling (available on request), and the SOC 2 appendix describing multi-tenant controls.

- Private (VPC / On-prem): Customer owns the control plane or runs a Private control plane under a support contract. Customer is responsible for network, OS patching (if on-prem), and KMS/HSM integration for key custody. Redwood provides integration guides and an HSM/KMS reference architecture. Evidence: hosted-dedicated-private-matrix.pdf (Private row), redwood-network-diagram.png (private subnet example), and our integration checklist.

2) KMS and key custody:
- Hosted: keys managed by Redwood; we use customer-provided envelope keys via external KMS integrations for enterprise customers where required (we support AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure KeyVault).
- Dedicated: default is Redwood-managed keys; customers can opt for customer-managed keys (CMK) where available.
- Private: customer-managed KMS/HSM is standard.

3) Control plane access & telemetry:
- Hosted: Redwood control plane handles orchestration, but we log control-plane operations; customers receive audit events and token-level traces.
- Dedicated: control plane is multi-tenant for orchestration by default; you can contract for reduced telemetry sharing.
- Private: control plane lives in customer environment or private control plane; Redwood operations access is controlled by support agreements and escrowed access procedures.

4) Artifacts we attached (see links / attachments):
- hosted-dedicated-private-matrix.pdf (concise table you can paste into SIG answers)
- redwood-network-diagram.png (shows Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private network flows)
- redwood-soc2-report-2026.pdf (scope and relevant controls)

I've attached the one-page matrix and the network diagram to this thread for immediate use. If you need quoted language for SIG Q3.1–3.6 I can supply a text block that matches our policy language exactly.

Best,

Irene Choi

Alex — quick technical clarifications to add to the SIG answers: 

- Network egress and data residency: For Hosted and Dedicated deployed in a region, inference data does not leave the selected region unless configured for cross-region replication or for model/catalog updates. Private deployments are controlled by your VPC/on-prem networking.

- Encryption-in-use / KV cache: All model KV caches are stored in memory on the serving host and are not persisted to shared storage. In Dedicated, the KV cache lives on the tenant-dedicated host; in Hosted, it's per-tenant in-process memory. If you have regulatory needs to avoid ephemeral caching, we can enable stricter cache retention policies via configuration.

- Access for incident response: For Hosted, our SRE runbooks include role-based temporary access, logged and time-limited. For Dedicated we can restrict support ACLs; Private follows the customer's access model with Redwood access via a support contract and just-in-time access tooling.

If you want, I can produce a short bullet list for the SIG column that references specific control IDs in the SOC 2 report (e.g., CC5.1 for encryption-at-rest, CC8.3 for logging).

-Marcus
Senior Product Engineer, Serving Runtime
Redwood Inference
